**The Last Day of the Pool**

The municipal pool closes on the first Sunday after Labor Day, and every year on that day the same thing happens: people who have not come all summer show up. They arrive at nine, when the gate opens, carrying towels that still have the crease from the shelf. They lie down on the concrete like they've been doing it for months. The lifeguards, who are mostly seventeen, look at them with something between contempt and tenderness. It's the last day. Everyone is allowed.

Marisol had worked the snack window for four summers. She knew the regulars by their orders. The man who got two frozen Snickers and ate them both before he reached his chair. The twins who shared one bag of Fritos and fought over who held it. The old woman who came at exactly two o'clock, bought a coffee nobody else would want in that heat, and drank it in the shade with her feet in the shallow end. Marisol never learned her name. She thought of her as the Coffee Lady and worried, each June, whether she'd come back.

On the last day, the Coffee Lady came at two.

"Same," she said.

"You know it's the last day," Marisol said, pouring.

"I know. That's why I'm here." She took the cup. "I'm here every day. But today I'm *here.*"

Marisol thought about that for the rest of her shift. The difference between being somewhere and being *there*. How the last of anything makes it suddenly visible. The pool had been blue all summer and she'd stopped seeing it by July. Now, at four in the afternoon on the last Sunday, it was so blue it hurt—that impossible chemical blue, the color of a thing that will not exist tomorrow.

---

I think about this a lot: how endings are the only reliable way we've found to pay attention.

We're bad at valuing what's ongoing. The ongoing has no edges, and we see with edges. A river you cross every day is just the way to work until the bridge closes for repairs, and then you find yourself standing at the detour looking down at the water, actually looking, for the first time in years. The last week of a job. The last night in an apartment when everything is in boxes and the rooms sound different. Nobody's ever more present in a house than when they're leaving it.

There's a version of this insight that's a cliché—*live every day like it's your last*—and it doesn't work, because it can't. If every day were the last, no day would be. The visibility depends on the contrast. You need the long blur of ordinary Tuesdays for the final Sunday to glow.

So maybe the trick isn't to make everything an ending. Maybe the trick is smaller: to remember, occasionally, that the ordinary is where nearly everything happens. That the season is made of the days you weren't paying attention. That the Coffee Lady was there every day, whether Marisol noticed or not, and that her being *there* on the last day was not the pool's doing but her own.

---

At six, the head lifeguard blew the whistle three times, the signal that meant everyone out for the year. The people who had come only today stood up slowly, gathering towels that were still mostly dry. The twins had to be called twice. Someone's kid cried.

Marisol closed the metal shutter on the snack window and counted the drawer. She'd done it a few hundred times. This time she counted slowly, noticing the weight of the quarters, the softness of the ones. Not because she was sentimental about money. Because it was the last time, and she wanted to have done it once with her whole attention, so that all the other times would have counted too. As though attention could work backward. As though noticing something at the end could retroactively make you have been present for the middle.

I don't know if that's true. I suspect it isn't. But I think the wish behind it is one of the most human things there is: the wish to have been there for our own lives.

---

The Coffee Lady was the last one through the gate. She'd stayed in the shade until the lifeguards started stacking chairs. She walked past the snack window on her way out, holding her empty cup, and stopped.

"See you in June," she said.

Marisol wasn't sure she'd be back. She was starting somewhere in the fall, a different city. The pool would hire someone else for the window, some fifteen-year-old who would learn the orders and stop seeing the blue by July.

"See you in June," she said anyway.

Because that's the other thing about endings: they don't ask permission to be endings. You often don't know. You think you'll be back and you aren't; you think it's the last time and it's not. The Coffee Lady would come at two o'clock next summer and ask for a coffee from a stranger, and maybe she'd say *same* out of habit, and the stranger would say *same what?*, and that would be its own small last day, unmarked, unnoticed by anyone but her.

Or maybe not. Maybe Marisol would be back. Maybe the new city wouldn't take. The future is where the endings hide, and you find them mostly in retrospect, walking past and thinking: *oh. That was it.*

---

They drained the pool on Tuesday. By Thursday it was a concrete bowl with a puddle at the deep end and a few leaves already collecting there, and a chain on the gate, and a sign that said SEE YOU NEXT SUMMER in letters that had faded a little more each year.

In June, they'd fill it again. The water would go in clear and turn blue when the light hit it. Someone would open the snack window. Someone would come at two o'clock and ask for coffee.

And for a few weeks, before the season blurred, everyone would see it.
